coachingPrompts: Where are the two candidate targets?

decisionProcess: Measure their separation and defensive routes.

en-US.explanation: A second target matters when distance forces the defending king to choose between two responsibilities. Two weak pawns are not automatically two targets: one route or central square may cover both. In pawn endings, use a remote passer or fixed weakness to draw the king away, then approach the other wing. Calculate chase, return, and entry squares rather than invoking a universal two-weakness rule.
keyIdeas: Distance matters only when one defensive route cannot serve both targets in time.
The attacking king needs a concrete entry created by the defender’s diversion.
misconceptions: Two weaknesses do not always win when one king route covers both.
Creating a remote pawn is pointless if no opposite-wing entry exists.
practicalRules: Create targets on separated wings when the defender cannot shuttle between them.
Approach the target whose defense most restricts the enemy king.
reflectionPrompts: What central square would make the two targets false?
Which target should be approached first and why?
